prompt: Hana asked 30 students for their favourite sport. Which display is the best choice for her data?

options.text: A bar graph
A scatter plot
A histogram
A time-series graph

feedback.b: A scatter plot needs two numerical variables for each person. Favourite sport is categorical.
feedback.c: A histogram is for numerical data grouped into intervals. Favourite sport is categorical.
feedback.d: A time-series graph shows how something changes over time.

hints: Is favourite sport a categorical or a numerical variable?
solution: Favourite sport is a **categorical** variable, so a **bar graph** (one bar per sport) is the best choice. A frequency table would also work.

prompt: Match each display to the kind of data it suits best.

right.text: Two numerical variables for the same people

left.text: Box plots on the same scale

right.text: Comparing a numerical variable for two groups

hints: Think about how many variables each display shows, and whether they are categorical or numerical.
solution: Scatter plot: two numerical variables. Two-way table: two categorical variables. Time-series graph: one variable over time. Box plots: comparing groups on a numerical variable. Bar graph: one categorical variable.

prompt: Tama wants to see whether the number of hours students study affects their test score. He will draw a scatter plot. Which is correct?

options.text: Hours of study on the x-axis, test score on the y-axis
Test score on the x-axis, hours of study on the y-axis
Both variables on the x-axis
Student names on the x-axis, test score on the y-axis

feedback.b: The test score is the response: it might depend on study time. The response variable goes on the y-axis.
feedback.c: A scatter plot has one variable on each axis.
feedback.d: That would be a bar graph of scores, not a scatter plot. It can't show a relationship between two variables.

hints: Which variable might explain or influence the other?
solution: Hours of study might explain the test score, so it is the **explanatory variable** (x-axis). The test score is the **response variable** (y-axis).

prompt:
Some students were asked whether they have a part-time job. The two-way table has some missing entries.

| | Job | No job | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Year 12** | 14 | ? | 40 |
| **Year 13** | ? | 12 | ? |
| **Total** | 37 | ? | 75 |

How many Year 13 students were surveyed?
hints: The two row totals must add up to the overall total.
You could also find the Year 13 "Job" entry from the "Job" column first.
solution:
Year 13 total $= 75 - 40 = 35$.

Check: Year 13 with a job $= 37 - 14 = 23$, and $23 + 12 = 35$ ✓.

prompt: A box plot has a very long right whisker and a short left whisker. What does this tell you?

options.text: The top quarter of the values are more spread out than the bottom quarter.
More values are in the right whisker than in the left whisker.
The mean is in the right whisker.
The data must have been recorded incorrectly.

feedback.b: Each whisker holds about a quarter of the values. Length shows spread, not how many values there are.
feedback.c: A box plot doesn't show the mean at all.
feedback.d: Uneven whiskers are common in real data. They just show that the data is not symmetrical.

hints: Each section of a box plot holds about 25% of the values.
solution: Both whiskers hold about 25% of the values. A longer right whisker means the top quarter of the values are **more spread out** (stretched over a bigger range), not that there are more of them.

prompt: Which is the best description of how to draw a line of best fit on a scatter plot?

options.text: A straight line that follows the trend, with about the same number of points above and below it
A line that joins the first point to the last point
A line that must start at the origin (0, 0)
A line that passes through as many points exactly as possible, even if it misses the trend

feedback.b: The first and last points might be unusual. The line should fit all the points, not just two.
feedback.c: A line of best fit doesn't have to go through the origin. It should go wherever the data is.
feedback.d: Hitting points exactly isn't the goal. The line should show the overall trend of all the points.

hints: The line should represent the overall pattern of all the points.
solution: A line of best fit is drawn by eye through the **middle of the points**, following the trend, with roughly equal numbers of points on each side. It doesn't need to go through the origin or through particular points.

prompt:
A histogram shows students' travel times in three intervals:

| Travel time (min) | 0–10 | 10–20 | 20–30 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 4 | 9 | 7 |

Ana says, "The mode is 9." What is wrong with her statement?

options.text: 9 is the frequency. The most common interval (the modal class) is 10–20 minutes.
Nothing: 9 is the largest number in the table.
The mode should be 20, because it is the highest time shown.
A histogram can't have a mode.

feedback.b: 9 tells you how many students are in the tallest bar. It isn't a travel time.
feedback.c: The mode is about the most common values, not the highest values.
feedback.d: Grouped data has a modal class: the interval with the highest frequency.

hints: Is 9 a travel time, or a count of students?
solution: 9 is a **frequency** (9 students), not a travel time. The interval with the highest frequency is **10–20 minutes**, so that is the **modal class**.

prompt: Wiremu wants to compare the travel times of students who walk to school with students who catch the bus. Which display would show the comparison most clearly?

options.text: Two box plots, one above the other, on the same scale
A scatter plot of walking time against bus time
A bar graph with one bar for each student
A two-way table of travel time against way of travel

feedback.b: Each student either walks or catches the bus, so there are no pairs of values to plot.
feedback.c: One bar per student makes a long, hard-to-read graph and doesn't summarise either group.
feedback.d: Travel time is numerical, so a two-way table (for two categorical variables) isn't suitable.

hints: You are comparing one numerical variable across two groups.
solution: Comparing a numerical variable for two groups is easiest with **box plots (or dot plots) on the same scale**, one above the other. You can compare the medians, the IQRs and the overall spread directly.

prompt:
A school library recorded how many books were borrowed each term.

| Year | Term 1 | Term 2 | Term 3 | Term 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 420 | 480 | 510 | 350 |
| 2024 | 450 | 520 | 540 | 380 |
| 2025 | 490 | 550 | 580 | 400 |

This data would be shown on a time-series graph. Describe the **trend** and any **repeating pattern** in the data. Use numbers from the table as evidence.
modelAnswer:
Trend: the number of books borrowed is increasing over time. For example, Term 1 loans rose from 420 in 2023 to 450 in 2024 and 490 in 2025, and every term was higher in 2025 than in 2023.

Repeating pattern: each year loans rise from Term 1 to a peak in Term 3 (510, 540 and 580), then drop to their lowest in Term 4 (350, 380 and 400).

rubric.criterion: Describes the upward trend over the three years
Describes the repeating pattern within each year (peak in Term 3, lowest in Term 4)
Supports both statements with numbers from the table

hints: Compare the same term across different years to see the trend.
Compare the terms within one year to see the repeating pattern.
solution: **Trend:** loans increase each year (e.g. Term 3: 510 → 540 → 580). **Repeating pattern:** within every year, loans are highest in Term 3 and lowest in Term 4 (e.g. 2025: 580 in Term 3, 400 in Term 4).

prompt:
A histogram shows the heights of 30 Year 9 students, but one bar has been rubbed out.

| Height (cm) | 140–150 | 150–160 | 160–170 | 170–180 | 180–190 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 4 | 9 | ? | 6 | 2 |

Which class interval contains the **median** height?

options.text: It's impossible to tell without the missing bar

feedback.b: Only 13 students are shorter than 160 cm, so the 15th and 16th heights are further along.
feedback.c: 13 students are shorter than 160 cm and 22 are shorter than 170 cm, so the 15th and 16th heights come before 170 cm.
feedback.d: You can find the missing frequency, because the frequencies must add up to 30.

hints: The frequencies must add up to 30. Find the missing one first.
With 30 values, the median is halfway between the 15th and 16th values. Use running totals.
solution:
Missing frequency: $30 - (4 + 9 + 6 + 2) = 9$.

Running totals: 4 (up to 150 cm), 13 (up to 160 cm), 22 (up to 170 cm), 28 (up to 180 cm), 30.

The median is halfway between the 15th and 16th heights. Both are in the **160–170 cm** class, because 13 students are shorter than 160 cm and 22 are shorter than 170 cm.

feedback.b: A line of best fit follows the trend of all the points. One unusual point shouldn't drag the line towards it.
feedback.c: Height is on the horizontal axis. P is at about 150 cm, so this is one of the shorter students.
feedback.d: Unusual points shouldn't be deleted just because they don't fit. Check first: it might be a recording mistake, or a real but unusual student.

hints: Read P's height and arm span from the axes.
What arm span does the line predict for that height?
solution: P is at a height of 150 cm and an arm span of 172 cm. The line predicts about 155 cm for that height, so P is about 17 cm above the trend. It is an **unusual point** (an outlier). The class should check the measurement: perhaps 152 cm was written down as 172 cm. If the measurement is correct, the point stays in the data.

prompt: Which display is drawn directly from the **five-number summary** of a data set?

options.text: Box plot
Dot plot
Histogram
Scatter plot

feedback.b: A dot plot shows every value. You can work out the five-number summary from it, but it doesn't show the summary directly.
feedback.c: A histogram shows how many values are in each interval.
feedback.d: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numerical variables.

hints: The five-number summary is the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum. Which display marks exactly these five values?
solution: A **box plot** is drawn from the five-number summary: the whiskers go out to the minimum and the maximum, the box goes from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, and a line inside the box marks the median.

prompt: What type of graph shows how one variable changes over time, with time along the horizontal axis and the points joined by lines?
hints: It has the same name as the type of investigation that looks at changes over time.
solution: A **time-series graph** shows one variable over time. Time goes along the horizontal axis, and the points are joined so you can see the trend and any repeating patterns.

prompt: In a histogram the bars touch, but in a bar graph there are gaps between the bars. Why do the bars of a histogram touch?

options.text: The data is numerical, and each interval starts where the last one ended (e.g. 10–20, then 20–30).
The data is categorical, so the categories run into each other with no gaps.
The bars touch to show that all the intervals have the same frequency.
The bars touch so that more of them can fit across the graph.

feedback.b: It's the other way round: bar graphs are for categorical data, which is why their bars are separate.
feedback.c: The bars of a histogram can have very different heights (frequencies).
feedback.d: The bars touching has a meaning. It isn't to save space.

hints: What is along the horizontal axis of a histogram: categories, or a number scale?
solution: A histogram shows **numerical** data grouped into intervals along a number line. Each interval ends where the next one begins (e.g. 10–20, then 20–30), so the bars touch. A bar graph shows separate **categories** (like favourite sports), so its bars have gaps.

prompt: Kai is drawing a dot plot of the number of push-ups his classmates did in one minute. The smallest number was 3 and the largest was 48. Which scale for the horizontal axis is the most suitable?

options.text: From 0 to 50, marked every 5
From 0 to 10, marked every 1
From 0 to 500, marked every 100
Only the numbers his classmates did, evenly spaced

feedback.b: This stops at 10, so most of the data (up to 48) wouldn't fit.
feedback.c: This is far too big: all the dots would be squashed into the first tenth of the axis.
feedback.d: A scale must go up in equal steps. Spacing only the data values evenly would make the gaps between them look wrong.

hints: The scale must fit all the data from 3 to 48, and go up in equal steps.
solution: A good scale covers all the data (3 to 48), isn't much bigger than it needs to be, and goes up in equal steps. From 0 to 50, marked every 5, does all three.

prompt:
80 students were asked whether they have a pet. There were 40 Year 9 students and 40 Year 10 students, and 45 of the 80 students have a pet. Of the students who have a pet, 60% are in Year 9.

How many Year 10 students do **not** have a pet?
hints: Draw a two-way table with rows for Year 9 and Year 10, columns for "Pet" and "No pet", and totals.
Start by finding how many Year 9 students have a pet: 60% of the 45 students with a pet.
Then fill in the rest of the table using the totals.
solution:
Year 9 students with a pet: 60% of 45 $= 0.6 \times 45 = 27$.

Year 10 students with a pet: $45 - 27 = 18$.

Year 10 students without a pet: $40 - 18 = 22$.

| | Pet | No pet | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Year 9** | 27 | 13 | 40 |
| **Year 10** | 18 | 22 | 40 |
| **Total** | 45 | 35 | 80 |

Check: the "No pet" column adds to $13 + 22 = 35$, and $80 - 45 = 35$ ✓

prompt: In a box plot, the median line is at the right-hand end of the box, in the same place as the upper quartile. There is a long whisker to the right of the box. What does this tell you about the data?

options.text: Many values are equal to the median, so the median and the upper quartile are the same value.
None of the values in the data set are greater than the median.
The box plot must have been drawn wrongly, because this can't happen.
The data doesn't have an upper quartile, so it is drawn at the median.

feedback.b: The long right whisker shows there are values above the upper quartile, so some values are greater than the median.
feedback.c: This can happen with real data. For example, 2, 3, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 9 has a median of 6 and an upper quartile of 6.
feedback.d: Every data set has an upper quartile. Here it just happens to be equal to the median.

hints: The part of the box between the median and $Q_3$ normally holds about a quarter of the values.
If that part of the box has no width, what must those values be?
solution:
Normally about a quarter of the values lie between the median and $Q_3$. If the median and $Q_3$ are the same, all of those values must be equal to the median, so that value is very common.

Example: 2, 3, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 9. The median is $\frac{6 + 6}{2} = 6$. The upper half is 6, 6, 6, 9, so $Q_3 = \frac{6 + 6}{2} = 6$. The whisker goes out to 9.
